title: The Great Reversal at Camiral
theme: Everything in TEG 18 came back to front: the man with three Wooden Spoons won the Trophy, the defending champion took the Spoon, and the reigning Spoon holder won the Green Jacket — a tournament in which the established order was not so much overturned as politely handed its coat.
opening_hook: Open at the end, on the presentation table: the TEG 18 Trophy going to Alex Baker, owner of three Wooden Spoons and two of them in the last three TEGs, standing next to his brother Jon Baker — defending champion, now holding this one's Spoon. Then rewind to the 5th hole of R1, where the Trophy was already effectively settled.

trophy_storyline.subject: Alex Baker, three-time Spoon collector, leads the TEG 18 Trophy from the 5th hole of R1 to the end despite a course-worst 106 and two double-figure holes
trophy_storyline.why_it_matters: The Trophy was won on the opening afternoon and defended by attrition: Alex Baker had one prior Trophy win and three Wooden Spoons, two of them in the last three TEGs, and this is the reversal the whole report hangs on.
trophy_storyline.shape: Alex Baker opened with 46 points on the Tour course, took the Trophy lead outright at the 5th in R1 (after two routine exchanges with David Mullin before it) and led by 12, having piled up 17 points across holes 8-12 and 13 more across 14-16. The turn is that he never played like that again: a 106 gross in R2 — a new course-worst at the Tour, exceeding the prior worst of 105 across 22 prior visits — including an 11 at the 18th, then a 10 at the 14th and an 8 at the 17th in R4. Yet the lead only ever narrowed from 12 to 11 to 12 to 8: he answered R2 with 21 points across holes 11-16 in R3, John Patterson outscored him over two of the four rounds and still lost by 8, and Alex Baker never finished a round worse than 3rd of 5.
headline_candidates: Alex Baker Wins It in Round One
From Two Spoons to the Trophy
trophy_storyline.chosen_headline: Alex Baker Wins It in Round One
trophy_storyline.standfirst: Twelve points clear after a 46 on the Tour course, the three-time Spoon holder spent the next three rounds handing it back in instalments — and never quite ran out.

jacket_storyline.subject: Gregg Williams, reigning Wooden Spoon holder, recovers from a ruinous R1 to take the TEG 18 Green Jacket by 14 from nine-time winner David Mullin
jacket_storyline.why_it_matters: Williams arrived holding the TEG 17 Wooden Spoon and left with the gross title at +66 — his best gross total in any TEG — taken off the man with nine prior Jacket wins.
jacket_storyline.shape: R1 on the Tour course was carnage: a 9 at the 7th, an 8 at the 17th, three holes from the 3rd to the 5th without a net par and 8 shots bled in the process, and by the 14th he was bottom of the Spoon race. A birdie at the 15th stopped the bleeding, and R2 came back 11 points better — 9 points across holes 3-5, 13 across 13-16 and four holes without dropping a gross shot — drawing level for the gross lead three separate times before taking it outright at the 2nd hole of R3. From there he never gave it back: four clean holes from the 2nd to the 5th in R3, 9 points across 8-10 in R4, and an 84 at the Stadium in R4, a personal best there by 8 shots, to win by 14.
headline_candidates: Nine at the Seventh, Jacket by Fourteen
From Spoon Holder to Jacket Winner
Williams Takes the Gross at the Second
jacket_storyline.chosen_headline: Nine at the Seventh, Jacket by Fourteen
jacket_storyline.standfirst: Gregg Williams turned up as the reigning Wooden Spoon holder and left with the gross title prised off David Mullin, who has won it nine times.

spoon_storyline.subject: Jon Baker, defending Trophy champion, leads the gross for 20 holes and then finishes the TEG 18 Wooden Spoon 23 points adrift of anyone else
spoon_storyline.why_it_matters: Jon Baker won both the Trophy and the Green Jacket at TEG 17; a year later he is last in three of four rounds and 23 behind the next worst, while his brother lifts the Trophy.
spoon_storyline.shape: He led the gross from the 5th hole of R1 and held it for 20 holes across two rounds, and closed R2 with 16 points over the last five holes without dropping a single gross shot — the one stretch all tournament that looked like a defending champion. He lost the gross lead at the 7th in R2, and then the Stadium took him apart: a 9 at the 4th in R3, bottom of the Spoon race from the 2nd hole of that round onwards, 8 shots gone across 15-18 in R3 and 10 more across 7-11 in R4 with five holes in a row without a net par. He finished on 126 points, 23 behind David Mullin, last in the field in three of the four rounds.
headline_candidates: Jon Baker Leads, Then Falls 23 Behind
Twenty Holes in Front, Four Days Adrift
spoon_storyline.standfirst: Jon Baker led the gross for 20 holes and collected the TEG 18 Wooden Spoon by 23 points, which in a field of five takes some doing.

discovered_storylines.subject: David Mullin takes 11 at the 15th in R1, then breaks the Stadium course record with 84 in R3, then bleeds it away over the closing stretch of R4
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: The lowest round ever recorded at the Stadium across 28 TEG visits, sandwiched between an eleven and a four-hole collapse — and it still was not enough to keep the Green Jacket.
discovered_storylines.shape: Mullin's TEG began with a sextuple-bogey 11 at the 15th in R1, his worst-ever score on a par 5, which dropped him straight to the bottom of the Spoon race from second. Two days later he went round the Stadium in 84 gross — a new course record, beating the prior best of 89 across 27 prior visits, and a personal best there by 7 shots. It bought him nothing: over holes 14-17 in R4 he dropped 9 shots and went four holes without a net par, and the Jacket went to Gregg Williams by 14.
headline_candidates: Mullin Rewrites the Stadium Course Record
The Best Round Ever Played Here
discovered_storylines.standfirst: David Mullin took eleven shots at the 15th on the opening day and, two rounds later, went round the Stadium in fewer than anyone has managed in 27 previous TEG visits.

discovered_storylines.subject: John Patterson loses the TEG 18 Trophy on the front nine of R1, bleeding 22 shots in eight holes, then spends three rounds proving he was the better player
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: Patterson finished 8 behind having outscored the champion over two of the four rounds — the entire deficit was posted before lunch on the opening day.
discovered_storylines.shape: From the 3rd to the 10th in R1 he dropped 22 shots — an 8 at the 3rd, a triple at the 2nd-hardest hole, seven consecutive holes without a net par — and was bottom of the Spoon race by the 4th. He then played like the best man in the field: 13 points across 13-16 to make R1 a 14-point back-nine improvement, 16 points across 11-15 in R2 despite an 8 at the 4th, 9 points across 4-6 in R4 and a birdie at the 17th to stop a late slide, with new personal bests at both the Tour (94) and the Stadium (93). It bought him second place and nothing else: even an ordinary round in place of his worst would still have left him short.
headline_candidates: Twenty-Two Shots Gone by the Tenth
discovered_storylines.chosen_headline: Twenty-Two Shots Gone by the Tenth
discovered_storylines.standfirst: John Patterson outscored the champion over two of the four rounds and still lost by eight, all of it conceded on one stretch of the Tour course on the opening day.

discovered_storylines.subject: A catalogue of the TEG 18 double-figure and blow-up holes: two elevens, a ten, two nines and a new course-worst gross at the Tour
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: Four of the five players posted a hole of quadruple bogey or worse, and the tournament produced both the lowest and the highest rounds in the history of these two courses.
discovered_storylines.shape: It opens on the Tour course, where David Mullin took 11 at the 15th, Gregg Williams took 9 at the 7th and 8 at the 17th, and John Patterson took 8 at the 3rd. It escalates in R2, where Alex Baker went 8 at the 16th and 11 at the 18th on his way to a 106 — a new course-worst at the Tour, exceeding the prior worst of 105 across 22 prior visits. It closes on the Stadium, with Jon Baker's 9 at the 4th in R3 and Alex Baker's 10 at the 14th and 8 at the 17th in R4, the latter two belonging to the eventual champion.
headline_candidates: The Holes That Stopped Being Golf
discovered_storylines.standfirst: An inventory of the holes where PGA Catalunya stopped being a golf course and became an administrative problem — two of the worst of them belonging to the winner.

vehicle_fit_response.note: The blow-up count is real and gets its own sidebar, but the frame is the reversal: Alex Baker's three Spoons to a Trophy, Jon Baker's title defence to the Spoon, Gregg Williams's Spoon to the Jacket.

why_the_champion_won: One enormous opening round — 46 points, best in the field — built a 12-point cushion Alex Baker then leaked slowly for three days without ever exhausting; he backed it with a second best-in-field round in R3, was the steadiest man in the field round to round, and John Patterson, who outscored him twice, had already bled 22 shots in eight holes on the first day.
